title: Embedded Feature Consumption Playbook - Runtime and Pricing Guidance
author: Marisol Gomez
content:
Overview:

This playbook documents recommended runtime behaviors, observability signals, and pricing considerations for customers embedding Redwood-powered features deeply inside their product UIs ("embedded features"). Embedded features are characterized by high request rates, short average prompt lengths, tight latency budgets (typically 50–300 ms P95), and heterogeneous quality requirements across routes. The guidance below is intended for product managers, platform engineers, and solutions teams planning migrations or new integrations that embed model inference into synchronous user flows.

Goals:

- Define predictable runtime and cost trade-offs for common embedding scenarios (search/snippets, autocomplete, summarization, conversational microflows).
- Provide a standardized set of per-route SLOs, telemetry, and sampling for quality checks.
- Provide recommended pricing/packaging options and migration steps for customers shifting to embedded consumption.

Scope:

- Applies to hosted Redwood API and Redwood Dedicated. Private deployments should follow the same SLO patterns but map to customer-specific capacity contracts.
- Focuses on text-generation and embeddings use cases; multimodal and heavy long-context pipelines require separate sizing guidance.

User personas and traffic patterns:

- Search snippet (high qps, short inputs, low per-request token budget). Typical pattern: 200–2,000 RPS for large tenants; average input 8–30 tokens; P95 latency target 100–200 ms.
- Autocomplete/typeahead (very low tolerance for latency spikes). Typical pattern: 100–20,000 events per minute per product; average input 4–12 tokens; P95 latency target 50–120 ms.
- Micro-conversation step (contextual user message plus short system directives). Typical pattern: bursty requests with low to medium token counts; P95 latency 150–300 ms.

Success metrics (product + platform):

- Latency: P95 < configured route SLO (default 200 ms for snippets, 100 ms for autocomplete).
- Cost: per-10k token unit cost within target band for route tier (see Pricing guidance section).
- Quality: False-negative rate on relevance reranking flows < 3% for high-tier customers (measured via synthetic prompt sets).
- Availability: 99.95% route-level availability for Dedicated customers; 99.9% for hosted free-tier-type routes.

Routing & runtime recommendations:

1) Route-level service tiers and admission control:
- Define per-route SLO profile: {latency_budget, max_batch_delay_ms, kv_cache_policy, fallback_model_chain}.
- Admission control: for extremely latency-sensitive routes (autocomplete), enable single-request prioritization (no batching or max batch delay 3 ms) and maximum concurrency caps to avoid tail amplification.

2) Batching and batching windows:
- Small-window batching (2–8 ms) for short-token routes increases throughput with minimal tail latency impact for non-autocomplete routes.
- Use dynamic batching profiles per route: sample request lengths to pick between tiny-batches (N=1–4) or micro-batches (N=4–32) depending on load.

3) Cache policies and prefix caching:
- For snippet and search flows, enable prefix KV caching at the per-route policy level with TTLs of 5–15 minutes for stable prompts (e.g., FAQ templates).
- For autocomplete, use ephemeral caching optimized for user session affinity only.

4) Fallback strategies and loyalty chains:
- Define a two-step fallback: fast low-cost, lower-fidelity variant (quantized or smaller model) followed by a full-fidelity model if confidence threshold misses.
- Confidence signals: model log-prob aggregate, n-best scoring variance, and reranker agreement.

Observability & quality monitoring:

- Required telemetry per route:
  - Latency histograms (P50/P95/P99), request size distribution, token counts, batch sizes.
  - Model variant ID, quantization profile, kernel family, node type (dedicated/shared).
  - Quality sampling: 0.5–2% of requests routed to controlled eval pipeline for ground-truth scoring (A/B label harness).

- Alerts and dashboards:
  - Alert if route P95 exceeds configured budget for > 3 consecutive 1-minute windows.
  - Unit-cost drift alert: 20% deviation from historical median cost per 1M tokens over a 24-hour window.

Pricing & packaging guidance:

- Route-tiered consumption (recommended default):
  - Tier: autocomplete (latency-critical), snippets (balanced), background (best-effort).
  - Each tier maps to a cost multiplier and an SLO profile. Example (guideline):
    - Autocomplete: compute premium 1.8x, stricter concurrency, single-request priority.
    - Snippets: compute multiplier 1.0x, batching enabled with 3–8 ms windows.
    - Background: discounted 0.6x, higher batch delays and lower priority.

- Token bundling and crediting:
  - Offer per-route token credits so customers can meter autocomplete separately from background ingestion.
  - For Dedicated customers, support fractional capacity carve-outs for critical routes (guaranteed QPS slices).

- Pricing constraints and fairness safeguards:
  - Soft limits: default per-route qps and token caps to prevent cost runaway.
  - Bulk discounts apply when consistent monthly spend on a route exceeds commit bands (e.g., 50M tokens/month).

Migration & rollout playbook:

1) Discovery and sizing:
- Run a 7–14 day traffic capture with tracing enabled for candidate routes. Record token distributions, request interarrival times, and user-visible latency tolerance.

2) Pilot staging (canary):
- Stage 1: internal pilot routing 1–5% traffic to the embedded route using controlled traffic shaping. Monitor P95 latency and unit token cost.
- Stage 2: 10–25% external pilot for up to 72 hours. Run quality sampling at 2% and compare to baseline metrics.

3) Full rollout:
- Gradual increase in 10–20% increments with rollback gates at each step for latency and cost thresholds.
- Post-rollout 14-day observation with weekly quality report.

4) Migration checklist (summary):
- [ ] Capture traffic sample and attach to migration ticket.
- [ ] Define per-route SLO and pricing tier.
- [ ] Enable observability and quality sampling.
- [ ] Configure caching and batch profile.
- [ ] Run 72-hour canary.
- [ ] Complete billing mapping and token credit assignment.

Open questions & decisions needed:

- Default crediting model for multi-tenant customers with mixed route tiers (recommended: per-route subaccounts).
- How to price hybrid fallback chains (should we bill only the final executed model tokens or sum across attempted models?). Proposed: bill only the model that returned the final token stream; record attempted fallback attempts for audit.

Appendix A — Sample API route configuration (yaml-like):

Route: product.search.snippet
SLO:
  latency_budget_ms: 200
  max_batch_delay_ms: 6
  kv_cache_policy: session-stable
Pricing:
  tier: snippets
  token_credit_account: route-snippet-2028
Fallback chain:
  - variant: small-quantized-v2 (confidence_threshold: 0.08)
  - variant: base-rtx-fidelity-v1 (confidence_threshold: 0.0)

Appendix B — CLI commands for canary (example):

# Capture traffic sample
redwood capture traffic --route product.search.snippet --window 7d --out snippet-sample.tar.gz

# Start canary at 5%
redwood route update product.search.snippet --canary-percent 5 --variant base-rtx-fidelity-v1

# Enable quality sampling 2%
redwood route update product.search.snippet --quality-sample 0.02
